title: House Robber II
directAnswer: The houses form a circle, so house 0 and house n-1 are now adjacent — you can't rob both. Split into two linear House Robber subproblems: one over houses [0 .. n-2] and one over [1 .. n-1], and return the larger. Each linear pass is the O(1)-space rolling-variable DP, so the whole thing is O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Circular 1D DP — reduce to two linear runs
rules: The circle makes house 0 and house n-1 adjacent — they can **never both** be robbed.
Break the cycle by FIXING the choice on house 0: either it's out (consider [1 .. n-1]) or the last house is out (consider [0 .. n-2]).
Run the **linear** House Robber on each range and take the max — never write a special circular recurrence.
Single-house input is the trap: with `n == 1` both ranges are empty, so special-case it to return `nums[0]`.
Each linear pass is the same `rob1/rob2` rolling-variable DP — O(1) space, reused twice.
whenToUse: House Robber constraints, but the line is closed into a ring
A circular-array DP where the two endpoints conflict with each other
You can remove the wrap-around by fixing one endpoint's inclusion
Any 'cannot pick both ends' constraint that splits cleanly into two open cases
antiSignals: Houses are a straight line → plain House Robber, no split needed
Houses form a tree → House Robber III, post-order DP
More than two endpoints interact → the two-range trick won't cover all cases
You're counting circular arrangements, not maximizing → a different combinatorial DP
remember.takeaway: House Robber II teaches the canonical 'break the circle' move: a ring constraint where two ends conflict reduces to two linear problems with one end excluded each. Solve the hard variant by reusing the easy one twice — a reduction pattern that recurs all over circular-array DP.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that the only new wrinkle is the 0↔n-1 adjacency, and reduce the circular problem to two calls of the linear solver rather than inventing a fragile circular recurrence.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to handle the wrap-around inside a single DP pass (off-by-one nightmares), or forgetting the n == 1 special case where both ranges are empty.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the reduction crisply — 'fix whether house 0 is robbable, that breaks the cycle into two linear runs' — reuse the O(1) linear solver, and call out the single-house edge case before being asked.

problemStatement:
You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. This time the houses are arranged in a **circle** — the first and last houses are ***adjacent*** to each other.

As before, adjacent houses have connected security systems, so robbing two directly adjacent houses on the same night alerts the police.

Given the integer array `nums` of money in each house, return the ***maximum amount you can rob tonight without alerting the police***.
understanding: Same as House Robber — pick a max-money subset with no two adjacent houses — except the array is circular, so the first and last houses count as neighbors. The single new constraint is that houses 0 and n-1 can't both be chosen.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the first and last houses really adjacent?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the whole difference from House Robber I. Robbing house 0 forbids house n-1 and vice versa.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if there's only one house?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return nums[0]. With n == 1 there's no neighbor to conflict with, and the two-range reduction would produce empty ranges, so special-case it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about two houses?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: They're adjacent in a circle, so rob the larger one: max(nums[0], nums[1]). The two-range split handles this naturally.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can money be zero?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, values are 0..1000. A zero house never helps the total but still blocks its neighbors if 'robbed'.

examples.explanation: Can't rob houses 0 and 2 (now adjacent in the circle), so the best single choice is house 1 → 3.
Rob house 0 (1) and house 2 (3) → 4. They aren't adjacent even in the circle.
Rob just house 2 → 3. Houses 0 and 2 conflict, so we can't take 1 + 3.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. House Robber II reduces to two linear runs.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recursion With Endpoint Cases
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first to expose how the circle splits into two open-ended cases, then flag the exponential recursion before optimizing.
hints: The only new rule is that houses 0 and n-1 are adjacent. What if you simply forbade one of them up front?
Case A: pretend house 0 doesn't exist → rob the line [1 .. n-1]. Case B: pretend house n-1 doesn't exist → rob the line [0 .. n-2]. The circle can't beat both.
For each case, recurse exactly like linear House Robber: rob(i) = max(nums[i] + rob(i+2), rob(i+1)) bounded by that case's range.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each linear recursion branches into two per house → ~2ⁿ nodes, and we run it twice (still O(2ⁿ)). Recursion depth O(n) for the stack.
approaches.explanation:
The circular constraint sounds scary, but it collapses to a single observation: in any valid plan, **house 0 and house n-1 are never both robbed**. So enumerate the two ways to honor that: either we leave house 0 out (and the remaining houses `1 .. n-1` form a straight line) or we leave house n-1 out (houses `0 .. n-2` form a straight line). The optimal circular answer is the better of these two linear answers.

**The mental shift: break the cycle by fixing an endpoint.** A ring is hard because the two ends wrap into each other. The instant you *force* one end to be excluded, the wrap-around disappears and you're left with the plain line problem you already know how to solve. Two cases cover every possibility because at least one end must be missing.

**Why two cases, not three.** You might worry about the plan that robs neither end — but that plan is already a sub-case of *both* ranges, so it's covered. There's no scenario that escapes both `[0 .. n-2]` and `[1 .. n-1]`.

**Why we don't ship this.** Each linear recursion overlaps subproblems exponentially, exactly like House Robber I. Name the reduction, then cache it.
approaches.insight: The reduction is the whole trick: a closed loop with conflicting ends becomes two open lines, each missing one end. Solving the harder problem by calling the easier one twice is a reusable move — it shows you'd rather compose known solutions than reinvent a brittle special case.

approaches.name: Top-Down Memoization
approaches.whenToMention: The fix once the overlap is named — 'cache each suffix within a range so each linear pass is O(n)'.
hints: Within a single range, rob(i) returns the same value every time. Cache it.
Run memoized linear House Robber twice — once per range — with a fresh memo for each so indices don't collide between passes.
memo[i] = max(nums[i] + solve(i+2), solve(i+1)), bounded by the range's hi.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each range has at most n distinct subproblems solved once in O(1) → O(n) per pass, two passes → O(n) total. O(n) for the memo and recursion stack.
approaches.explanation:
Keep the two-range reduction, but memoize each linear pass so the exponential recursion becomes linear. For a given range, `solve(i)` caches the best loot achievable from house `i` to the range's end; the second time that suffix is needed it's a free read.

**The mental shift: memoize the inner problem, not the outer split.** The circular reduction is just two independent linear problems. We don't memoize across the split — each pass gets its own cache because index `i` means different things relative to each range. Inside a pass, the optimization is identical to House Robber I: cache `solve(i)` once.

**Why a fresh cache per range.** If both passes shared one memo, an answer computed for range `[0 .. n-2]` could be wrongly reused for range `[1 .. n-1]`, where the boundaries differ. Resetting the cache (or keying it by range) keeps the two passes correct and independent.

**Why the sentinel is -1.** Money can be 0, so 0 is a valid cached answer. Use -1 to mark 'not computed' so a genuine zero suffix isn't mistaken for a cache miss.
approaches.insight: Memoization here is layered on top of a reduction: solve the circle by reducing to lines, then make each line fast with a cache. Composing a problem-shape reduction with a standard speed-up is a very common interview move — recognize the sub-problem, then apply the textbook optimization to it.

approaches.name: Bottom-Up — Two Linear Passes, Two Variables Each (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Frame it as 'reuse the O(1) linear House Robber on two ranges and take the max'.
hints: You already have the O(1) rolling-variable linear House Robber. How many times do you need to call it for the circle?
Call it once on houses [0 .. n-2] and once on [1 .. n-1], then return the max. Don't allocate any DP array.
Each call keeps just rob1 and rob2; the single-house case returns nums[0] before the split.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Two linear scans, each O(n) with O(1) work per house → O(n) time. Each scan keeps two integers → O(1) space overall.
approaches.explanation:
Combine the reduction with the constant-space linear solver. Write a helper `robLinear(lo, hi)` that runs the familiar two-variable House Robber over an index range, then return `max(robLinear(0, n-2), robLinear(1, n-1))`. Guard `n == 1` up front so neither range is empty.

**The mental shift: compose, don't reinvent.** The optimal House Robber I is a five-line rolling loop. The circular version needs *nothing new* algorithmically — it just calls that loop twice over two ranges. Recognizing that the hard problem is two instances of the easy one is the entire interview signal here.

**Why this stays O(1) space.** Each linear pass keeps only `rob1` and `rob2`; we never materialize a `dp[]` array, and the two passes run sequentially, reusing the same two variables. So memory is constant regardless of how many houses there are.

**Why the single-house guard is non-negotiable.** With `n == 1`, the range `[0 .. n-2]` is `[0 .. -1]` and `[1 .. n-1]` is `[1 .. 0]` — both empty, so the helper would return 0 and you'd lose the lone house's money. Returning `nums[0]` before the split fixes it. (The two-house case is fine: ranges `[0..0]` and `[1..1]` correctly yield `max(nums[0], nums[1])`.)
approaches.insight: The constant-space trick from House Robber I carries over untouched — the circle only adds an outer 'try both endpoint exclusions' wrapper. When a follow-up adds a global constraint to a problem you've solved, ask whether you can express the constraint as a small set of restricted re-runs rather than a brand-new algorithm. That reframing turns 'medium' circular problems into two 'easy' linear ones.

pitfalls: Omitting the n == 1 guard — both ranges empty, returns 0 instead of the single house.
Building a full dp array per pass — wastes the O(1) space the rolling variables give you.
Returning rob1 instead of rob2 from robLinear — off-by-one excluding the last house in the range.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that house 0 and house n-1 are adjacent in the circle — produces House Robber I's answer.
Missing the n == 1 special case, where both reduced ranges are empty and the helper returns 0.
Trying to encode the wrap-around in one DP pass instead of splitting into two linear runs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ignoring the circular adjacency
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Running plain linear House Robber lets you rob both house 0 and house n-1, which the circle forbids. On [2,3,2] it would return 4 instead of 3.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the single-house guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With n == 1 the ranges [0 .. n-2] and [1 .. n-1] are both empty, so the helper returns 0 and the lone house's money is lost.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Overlapping both endpoints in a range
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If either range spans the full [0 .. n-1], the 0↔n-1 conflict comes back. Each range must exclude exactly one endpoint.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int a = robLinear(nums, 0, n - 1);
int b = robLinear(nums, 0, n - 1);
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int a = robLinear(nums, 0, n - 2);
int b = robLinear(nums, 1, n - 1);
